name: Priya Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing is linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm senior weaver at Ashby Mills, on the valley road. We weave tough technical fabric, the webbing for seatbelts and lifting straps, on rows of fast looms. I look after twelve looms on my shift: I tie in broken threads, change the beams of yarn, and catch faults before they run for a hundred metres. I like the rhythm of the shed and knowing every loom's little habits. What wears me out is the noise, and the night shift once a month.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to be the senior on your shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My aunt worked at Ashby for thirty years and got me in at eighteen. I did my technical diploma at night while working days. Now I train the new starters. I'm married to Daniel, he's an electrician, and we're hoping to start a family in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That would suit me fine. I've never thought a computer could tie in a broken thread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's like every other fad, a bit of use and then on with life. At work I'd tell the new starters that skill and hard work still count. I'd say much the same to my family on Sunday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved. Ashby has steady orders from the car industry, and I'm the senior on my shift. The only thing I watch is whether the car makers keep buying from us or go abroad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am and keep saving about £250 a month. Daniel and I would try for a baby next year, as we planned. I'd keep using the AI app on my phone now and then for recipes and letters, nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Settled, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a baby mean for your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maternity leave, then back on days only, I'd hope. My mum's ten minutes away and has already offered to help. That's how my family's always done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about Ashby that worries you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The car makers squeeze our prices every year. If one of them moves its order abroad, we'd go on short weeks. But that's been true since my aunt's time.

say: I'd say AI was **a fad**, useful for a bit.
I'd tell new starters **skill and hard work** still count.
think: Ashby has **steady orders** and I'm senior on my shift.
The one thing I watch is car makers **moving orders abroad**.
do: Try for a **baby** next year as planned.
Use the **AI app** for recipes and letters only.
S0.quote: I've never thought a computer could tie in a broken thread.
fieldNote: She feels **secure**, with steady orders and a senior post.
Her plans centre on **starting a family** with her mother's help.
Her only standing worry is **car makers** moving orders abroad.

steps.text: Keep running twelve looms on the same shift
Save £250 a month for a family fund
Try for a baby with Daniel next year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the clever computer work first, and the robots creep in after. Hm. That sounds believable, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say at work that when the shuttle looms went, people learned the new ones. The mill will adapt like it always has. I'd tell friends to keep working hard and not wait for the government to sort it out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think my looms are safe for a while, because a robot that ties in threads is a long way off. But the planners and the order office will shrink, and then my shift gets run by a schedule on a screen. I'd want to be the one who understands that screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Once the other seniors had tried it, I'd learn the new loom monitoring software properly. I'd ask Ashby about their technician course, the one that teaches loom maintenance. And Daniel and I would still try for a baby, but maybe hold off a few months to save a bit more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. It's like a draught in the house, you notice it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for the other seniors to try the software first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Ashby has bought things before that didn't work. There was a camera system that kept stopping looms for nothing. I'd rather let someone else find the faults.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about at the mill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office ladies, honestly. Pat in orders has been there longer than me and doesn't drive. If her job goes, she hasn't got many options.

say: I'd say the mill will **adapt**, as it did when the shuttle looms went.
I'd tell friends to **keep working** and not wait for government.
think: My looms are **safe for a while**.
The **order office** will shrink and my shift will be run from a screen.
do: Learn the **loom monitoring software** after other seniors try it.
Hold off on a **baby** a few months to save more.
feel: **Uneasy**, like noticing **a draught** in the house.
S1.quote: When the shuttle looms went, people learned the new ones. The mill will adapt like it always has.
fieldNote: She draws on **mill history**, like the end of shuttle looms, for reassurance.
She'd move **after others** have tested new systems.
Her worry is for **office colleagues** like Pat.

steps.text: Learn the loom monitoring software after other seniors test it
Ask Ashby about the loom technician course
Delay trying for a baby a few months to save more

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? And robots by 2031. I'd be in the middle of having children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say nobody voted for this and the companies are moving too fast. At work I'd say we stick together and look after the young ones. At home I'd say we put family first and get through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the looms are gone by 2031. A robot that ties in threads would be expensive, but cheaper than three shifts of weavers. Daniel's work is safer, because wiring old houses is messy, so we'd lean on his wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the loom technician course straight away, before everyone else does, which isn't like me. We'd still have a baby, but sooner rather than later, so I'm on leave before the robots arrive. I'd save harder too, maybe £400 a month, cutting the second car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It's not my style to rush, and this would make me rush.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why have a baby sooner rather than later?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I'm going to lose the mill job in 2031, better to have had maternity pay from Ashby first. And my mum's healthy now. Five years from now, who knows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd lean on Daniel's wage. Is that comfortable for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's how my parents did it, so in a way, yes. But I'd want my own trade too. I don't like being dependent on anyone, even him.

say: I'd say **nobody voted** for this pace.
I'd tell colleagues to **stick together** and protect the young ones.
think: I expect my looms to be **gone by 2031**.
My husband Daniel's **electrician work** is safer, so we'd lean on it.
do: Have a **baby sooner** to use maternity pay first.
Save **£400 a month** by selling the second car.
S2.quote: If I'm going to lose the mill job in 2031, better to have had maternity pay from Ashby first.
fieldNote: She **expects to lose** her job but has her husband's safer wage.
She'd move a **baby forward**, a striking choice.
Speed overrides her usual **caution**, and she notices it.

steps.text: Enrol on Ashby's loom technician course straight away
Try for a baby sooner, while Ashby still pays maternity leave
Sell the second car and save £400 a month
Ask Mum to help with childcare so both of us work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, robots 2034. That's more my pace, I'll be honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready, and people shouldn't panic. I'd want apprenticeships for adults, not handouts. At church I'd say the same: plan, pray and work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd think I've got a good few years at the looms. I'd have my children, go back part-time, and train for loom maintenance before 2034. It still worries me, but there's time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait to see how the first technician course group gets on, then sign up around 2027. We'd have our first baby as planned. I'd keep using the AI app a bit more, maybe for the course work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. I can work with this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you sign up earlier?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Ashby put a robot on the first loom row. That would tell me it's real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Daniel have a view on it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My husband says I worry too much. He might be right. But he's not the one standing next to twelve looms.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough to get ready without panic.
I'd push for **adult apprenticeships**, not handouts.
At church I'd say **plan, pray and work**.
think: I've got **a good few years** at the looms.
I'd have children and train in **loom maintenance** before 2034.
do: Watch the first **course group**, then enrol around 2027.
Use the **AI app** for course work.
S3.quote: My husband says I worry too much. He might be right. But he's not the one standing next to twelve looms.
fieldNote: Her trigger to act is a **robot** on the first row of looms.
Her husband is **calmer** than she is.

steps.text: Enrol on the loom maintenance course around 2027
Have our first baby next year as planned
Use the AI app to help with course work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, robots in 2039. That's a lifetime in a mill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is manageable and we should just get on with it. At work I'd tell people to learn a second skill while there's time. I'd be calm about it, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd think the mill has most of a decade left. I'd have my children, work, and then move into maintenance or training. By 2039 my kids would be in school, and I'd be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Ashby and have our family as planned. Around 2032 I'd train in loom maintenance. I'd also start doing curtain and alteration work from home, because I can sew well and it's a bit of extra money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy now and then, but mostly settled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the sewing work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because people always need curtains taken up and dresses fixed. It's small money, but it's mine, and it's work a robot won't bother with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Ashby closed early for other reasons. Then the timeline doesn't matter.

I'd tell colleagues to learn **a second skill** while there's time.
think: The mill has **most of a decade** left.
I'd move into **maintenance or training** after having children.
By **2039** my children would be in school.
do: Keep going at **Ashby** and have our family.
S4.quote: People always need curtains taken up and dresses fixed. It's small money, but it's mine, and it's work a robot won't bother with.
fieldNote: She'd add a **home sewing** income for independence.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it would hit just as we start a family. What would help is paid adult apprenticeships and an honest timeline from Ashby so we can plan around the children.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about women in factories. A lot of us women in factories plan our families around shifts. If the shifts disappear, so does the plan.
